newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown tumbles after cen bank sets it free.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown tumbles after cen bank sets it free.

text.p: The Czech crown tumbled as expected on Tuesday after the central bank (CNB) allowed the currency to float, with dealers predicting further volatility in coming weeks.

Late on Monday, the central bank eliminated its fluctation band within which the crown moves against a mark/dollar basket, and said that decisive for the rate of the crown will now be its relation to the mark.
No details on how the crown would shadow the German mark were given.
At 1115 GMT, the crown was trading at 19.623 to the mark and 33.242 to the dollar, implying a deviation against its former basket of 11.78 percent below basket parity.
Before the central bank eliminated the +/-7.5 percent band, the crown was trading at -2.8 percent and was fixed against the mark at 18.078.
Currency traders said the move took the market by surprise, but that repeated central bank direct interventions and a choking of market liquidity were untenable in the long run.
"It was a bit of an unexpected move," said Pavel Pinkava of Nomura International.
"Generally speaking, I think the (crown) market is going to be difficult to stabilise now. We should find out tomorrow (Wednesday) how far lower the crown will be pushed," he added.
Prior to the announcement, the crown was fixed daily within a fluctuation band of plus or minus 7.5 percent against central parity with a basket of currencies comprised of the mark and dollar.
The Czech crown has been under heavy downward pressure recently, as speculators took advantage of a bulging current account and foreign trade deficits to challenge the central bank to intervene.
The central bank intervened on several occasions over the past 10 days to buy crowns to support the exchange rate.
In addition to scrapping the bands, the CNB also raised its key discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent on Monday, in an attempt to keep a tight grip on market liquidity.

After the CNB announcement, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus appealed for an end to the volatility in the crown's exchange rate, which had been continually pushed to record lows last week as the market and central bank battled for control of the currency.
"Let's seek a new balanced level of our exchange rate on the market. Let's not try to find any big danger in the movement of the exchange rate," Klaus said.
But dealers said the move to eliminate the band, which the central bank had said it expected to do sometime in the future, would probably not put an end to the unsettled situation.

"We expect huge volatility on the forex market...We would not be surprised to see the crown fall to 15 percent (ie. 35 crowns to the dollar and 20.5 crowns to the mark) within a few hours or days," said Vladimir Kreidl of Patria Finance.

Added one trader: "Ultimately speaking, the idea of keeping a dollar component probably wasn't a good idea in the long-run. The market will now over-react a bit and push the crown too far down, but then it should come back a bit."
